transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman.
Hundreds of people rallied in Ithaca, New York, Sunday
in support of a former Cornell University student
known as Jane Doe.
The woman says she was raped by several fraternity members
at an on-campus party in 2024.
Celia Clark with member station WSKG reports.
>> We believe you, Jane Doe.
>> People held signs saying essays are not punishment
for rape, and we are Jane Doe.
Elliott Larson is a student at neighboring Ithaca College
and one of the rally's organizers.
They say it's all for Jane Doe.
>> I feel like it's really important for her to see
that her community is standing with her
and we're standing behind her
and we don't accept the mishandling of her case
by Cornell.
>> New York Governor Kathy Hochul sent a message
that was read at the rally reiterating her commitment
to change state laws on sexual assault and consent.
More public protests in Ithaca are scheduled
over the next few weeks.
For NPR News, I'm Celia Clark in Ithaca.
>> Police in Georgia are still trying
to understand what led to a shooting early Sunday morning
at a homecoming party in the city of Vienna.
Two people were killed and almost three dozen others
were injured.
Police were patrolling the party, which extended for four blocks
when the shooting broke out.
There have been no arrests and so far no motive has been given.
Voters in Brazil will return to the polls on October 25th
for a run-off presidential election after no candidate
in Sunday's election reached more than 50% of the voting.
Incumbent Luis Inacio Lula da Silva
trails conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday's tally.
NPR's Carrie Khan has more.
>> Flavio Bolsonaro did very well over Lula,
losing ground in major states around the country.
This was Flavio Bolsonaro's first national election, too.
His father appointed him as the forebearer
of the Bolsonaro conservative movement,
and a lot of people were skeptical
since he's seen as not as charismatic or skilled
as his father, but he finished ahead of Lula
and goes into the run-off with huge political momentum.
>> That's NPR's Carrie Khan on Rio de Janeiro with our story.
Authorities in Japan have arrested a U.S. marine
in connection with the apparent murder of a woman
on the island of Okinawa,
and Pierre Scott Newman has her story.
>> Prefectural police arrested the 20-year-old marine
assigned to Okinawa's Fatemna Air Station.
According to Japan's Kyoto News Service,
authorities believe the marine robbed and strangled
a 39-year-old local woman at a hotel in the capital, Naha.
Okinawa's governor called the incident "absolutely unforgivable,"
and said Okinawans are "outraged."
About half of the 50,000 U.S. troops
stationed in Japan are in Okinawa.
Their presence has been a source of friction for years
with a number of high-profile murders and sexual assaults
involving American service members.
Scott Newman, NPR News.
>> And you're listening to "NPR News."
German Chancellor Friedrich Mertz
announced a new aid package for Ukraine Sunday.
The announcement came during a visit to Kyiv.
The package is valued at more than 1.3 billion euros,
with much of that for military assistance,
including combat drones and long-range strike weapons.
The Justice Department is moving hundreds of detainees
who are awaiting trial near Atlanta
to a detention center several hours away.
Legal groups and Democratic lawmakers
say the transfer unlawfully cuts people off
from their lawyers, NPR's Kristin Wright reports.
>> Attorneys for the detainees say the U.S.
Marshal Service's decision to move their clients
almost 200 miles to a detention center in South Georgia
separates them from family
and is a violation of their constitutional right
to legal counsel.
The detainees are all facing federal criminal cases.
The Marshal Service plans to transfer
about 400 people by the end of the month,
according to the non-profit federal defender program.
It tells NPR 20 to 30 of its clients
have already been moved.
The group's executive director says attorneys
traveling six hours round-trip
and meeting by video with clients
would restrict their right to counsel
and estimates it'll cost taxpayers.
Georgia Public Broadcasting reports
the Marshal Service said in a statement
the decisions based on, quote,
"diverse challenges" to ensure safe and secure confinement.
Kristin Wright, NPR News.
>> Irish players wore black armbands
and bowed their heads during the Israeli National Anthem Sunday
before their Second Nations League soccer match.
The Irish team was recognizing the lives
lost in Israel's war on Gaza.
The Israeli players also wore black armbands
in memory of people killed in the Hamas-led attacks in 2023.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
>> Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now
sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism
and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: Rally held in Ithaca, New York supporting Cornell student who alleges rape by fraternity members
Shooting at homecoming party in Vienna, Georgia kills two, injures nearly three dozen people
Brazil holds runoff presidential election October 25th after no candidate reached 50 percent Sunday
U.S. Marine arrested in Okinawa in connection with murder of local woman at hotel
German Chancellor Friedrich Mertz announces 1.3 billion euro aid package for Ukraine including military weapons
Justice Department transfers hundreds of federal detainees near Atlanta to distant South Georgia facility
Irish soccer team wears black armbands during Israeli National Anthem to recognize Gaza war deaths
